expect:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus encouraged private prayer in Matthew 6:6 — 'go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen' — suggesting a personal relationship with God is valued.
• Private worship allows Christians to express personal concerns and emotions freely without the pressure of a congregation.
• It can take place anywhere and at any time, making it more accessible than attending a church service.
• The quality of prayer may be deeper when a Christian is alone and undistracted.

Arguments against:
• Communal worship unites believers and creates a sense of community — Jesus said 'Where two or three gather in my name, there am I with them' (Matthew 18:20).
• Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a structured encounter with God through sacraments like the Eucharist.
• The Bible instructs Christians not to neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:25).
• Communal worship provides support, teaching and accountability that private worship cannot.

expect:
Arguments in support:
• Believers' baptism involves a personal, conscious decision — the person understands and chooses to commit to Christ, making the commitment more genuine.
• Jesus was baptised as an adult by John the Baptist (Matthew 3:13–17) — this is the biblical model for baptism.
• Full immersion powerfully symbolises dying to sin and being raised to new life in Christ, mirroring Jesus's death and resurrection.
• Babies cannot understand the promises being made on their behalf.

Arguments against:
• Infant baptism removes original sin — without it, Catholics believe a child would remain in a state of sin.
• Jesus said 'Let the little children come to me' (Mark 10:14), showing God's grace should be available to everyone from birth.
• Parents and godparents take responsibility for the child's spiritual development — this is a loving act of the faith community.
• The child can later confirm their faith through the sacrament of Confirmation.
• Most Christian denominations worldwide (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox, Methodist) practise infant baptism — it has centuries of tradition behind it.

expect:
Arguments in support:
• Pilgrimage has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity — it deepens faith and brings believers closer to God.
• Sites like Lourdes offer healing and spiritual renewal — over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.
• Jesus himself made pilgrimages to Jerusalem for Jewish festivals.
• Pilgrimage to places like Iona builds community and provides time for prayer and reflection away from daily life.

Arguments against:
• God is omnipresent — present everywhere — so He can be worshipped anywhere. There is no need to travel to a special place.
• Jesus taught that what matters is the quality of your faith, not where you worship: 'God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth' (John 4:24).
• Money spent on pilgrimage could be better used to help the poor — Jesus said 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me' (Matthew 25:40).
• Some Christians (e.g. many Protestants) do not practise pilgrimage at all and do not consider it necessary for salvation.

expect:
Arguments in support:
• Practical help meets immediate needs — food banks provide food for those in crisis, and street pastors protect vulnerable people at night. This follows Jesus's teaching: 'I was hungry and you gave me something to eat' (Matthew 25:35).
• Actions speak louder than words — the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) shows that true neighbourly love is about practical action, not just talking about faith.
• Helping locally builds trust in the community and can naturally lead to people asking about the Christian faith, without pressuring them.
• Some people are put off by direct evangelism and see it as intrusive.

Arguments against:
• Jesus specifically commanded his followers to evangelise — the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) says 'Go and make disciples of all nations.' This is a direct instruction that Christians must obey.
• Without evangelism, the Church would eventually die out — new believers are needed for the faith to survive and grow.
• Spreading the faith addresses people's spiritual needs, which Christians believe are even more important than physical needs — Jesus said 'What good is it for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul?' (Mark 8:36).
• The best approach combines both — mission includes both practical help AND sharing the gospel.
